::: {.lead}
Omar wants to copy the levels of *Pocket Quest* to a USB stick, and Windows
says "File too large". The stick has 16 GB free, and the file is only 5 GB.
Another player has a new gamepad that the game does not see. Both problems
come from a part of the operating system that most players never see: the
**file system** and the management of **devices**. In lectures 9 and 10 you
saw how the OS shares the CPU and the RAM. In this lesson you see how it
keeps files on a drive, why the format of a drive matters, and how it
manages devices and the other resources that games share. Every section ends
with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary file-system file-path file-extension file-metadata storage-block size-on-disk file-system-format system-resources device-driver plug-and-play usb-mode >}}

## 11.1 Where does a game keep its files?

A game is not one file. *Pocket Quest* on Windows has a program file, packs
of levels and music, and the save files of the player. The **file system**
keeps all of them in folders, and finds them by their **path** (@fig-files).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 11.1 — File system"}
The **file system** is the part of the OS that keeps files and folders on a
drive: their names, their places (paths), their sizes and their dates. The
data about a file (name, type, size, dates, permissions) is its
**metadata**.
:::

![The files of Pocket Quest on a Windows PC: the game folder, and the save files in the player's Documents.](images/game-files.png){#fig-files width=96%}

The **file extension** (.exe, .pak, .sav, .png) tells the OS and the player
what kind of file it is. A path like
`C:\Games\PocketQuest\Data\levels.pak` goes from the drive (C:) one folder
deeper at every `\`. Android and macOS write `/` instead of `\`.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.1 — Game files and player files"}
1. The game folder `C:\Games\PocketQuest` holds the program (80 MB) and the
   packs `levels.pak` (1.2 GB) and `music.pak` (320 MB). They are the same
   for every player.
2. The save file `slot1.sav` (2 KB) is in the player's own folder
   `C:\Users\Omar\Documents\PocketQuest\Saves`. It is different for every
   player.
3. When Omar reinstalls the game, the game folder is new, but his save file
   stays.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.2 — The same game on a phone"}
On a phone, each app has its own folder in its sandbox (lecture 10). The
player cannot open it; Settings shows only the size: app, user data and
cache (lecture 4).
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Looking for the save file in the game folder. Many PC games keep the
player's files in Documents or in a hidden AppData folder, so that they stay
when the game is updated.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The files of an app"}
On the lab computer, open File Explorer and go to `C:\Program Files`.

1. Open the folder of one program. Write the path, and the name and size of
   its biggest file.
2. Right-click the file › Properties. Write three items of its metadata.

*Your result:* one path, one file with its size, and three items of metadata.
:::

## 11.2 How files sit on a drive: blocks and formats

A drive is divided into **blocks** (also called clusters), often 4 KB each.
The file system gives every file whole blocks, so a small file wastes part
of its last block (@fig-blocks).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 11.2 — Block and size on disk"}
A **block** is the smallest piece of a drive that a file system gives to a
file (often 4 KB). The **size on disk** of a file is its size rounded up to
whole blocks.
:::

![A file always uses whole blocks. The rest of the last block is wasted.](images/blocks.png){#fig-blocks width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.3 — Many small files"}
An old version of Pocket Quest kept every tile as its own file: 10 000 files
of 1 KB. Blocks are 4 KB.

1. Data: 10 000 × 1 KB = 10 000 KB, about 10 MB.
2. On disk: 10 000 × 4 KB = 40 000 KB, about 39 MB.
3. Packed into one file of 10 000 KB, they need only 2 500 blocks: about
   10 MB. This is one reason why games use pack files (.pak).
:::

The **format** of a drive is the kind of file system on it. Different
systems use different formats (@tbl-formats).

| Format | Used on | Note for a game developer |
|---|---|---|
| NTFS | Windows drives | the game folder on a PC |
| exFAT | USB sticks, memory cards | works on Windows, Mac and Android; big files |
| FAT32 | old USB sticks | no file of 4 GB or more |
| APFS | iPhone, iPad, Mac | Apple devices |
| ext4 or F2FS | Android phones | Android devices |

: File system formats. {#tbl-formats}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.4 — File too large"}
Omar's old USB stick is formatted FAT32. FAT32 cannot keep one file of 4 GB
or more, so the 5 GB `levels.pak` does not fit, even with 16 GB free. After
formatting the stick as exFAT (which deletes what is on it), the copy works.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Thinking that free space is the only limit. The format can also limit the
size of one file (FAT32: under 4 GB).
:::

{{< sim file="sims/block-lab.html" poster="sims/block-lab.png" title="Block Lab: size and size on disk" height="560" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Size and size on disk"}
On the lab computer, make a text file with one short line (right-click on
the desktop › New › Text Document). Right-click it › Properties.

1. Write its "Size" and its "Size on disk". Why are they different?
2. In **Block Lab**, save ten small files and pack them. How many blocks do
   you save?

*Your result:* two sizes with a reason, and the blocks saved.
:::

## 11.3 Sharing the hardware: devices and resources

A gamepad, a headset, a camera and a USB cable are **devices**. The OS finds
them, loads their **drivers**, shares them between apps and checks
permissions. It also shares the other **resources**: CPU time, memory,
storage, battery and network (@fig-devices).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 11.3 — Device management"}
**Device management** is the job of the OS that finds connected devices
(**plug and play**), loads a **driver** for each one, gives apps access to
them in turn, and checks their permissions. The **system resources** that
the OS shares are CPU time, memory, storage, battery, network and devices.
:::

![A new gamepad: connect, detect, driver, ready. A phone asks what its USB cable may do.](images/device-management.png){#fig-devices width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.5 — A new gamepad"}
1. Ali connects the gamepad by USB. Windows detects it and loads a driver.
2. Device Manager shows it under Human Interface Devices. If it has a yellow
   warning sign, the driver is missing.
3. With a working driver, the game reads the buttons through the OS.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.6 — A phone on a USB cable"}
1. A phone connected to a PC charges, but the PC shows no files.
2. The phone shows a USB mode: charging only, file transfer or photos.
3. Choosing **file transfer** lets the PC see the phone's folders. An iPhone
   asks "Trust this computer?" first.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Blaming the game when a device does not work. If the OS does not see the
device, no game can use it: check the connection, the driver and the
permission first.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Connect your phone"}
Connect your phone to the lab computer with a USB cable.

1. What does the PC show? Change the USB mode on the phone to file transfer
   (iPhone: tap Trust).
2. In File Explorer, find the phone's folder of photos (Android: DCIM).

*Your result:* the USB modes your phone offers and the path of the photos.
:::

## Case study: Disk Doctor at Byte Bay

The team of *Byte Bay* collects file and device problems of *Pocket Quest*.
Omar's old FAT32 USB stick refuses the 5 GB `levels.pak`. Omar cannot find his
save file `slot1.sav`. An old version had 10 000 files of 1 KB on a drive
with 4 KB blocks, and the team packed the levels into one `levels.pak`.
Ali's new gamepad shows a yellow sign in Device Manager. And a 6 GB test build
must go on a USB stick that works on Windows and on a Mac. The Game challenge
of the interactive lesson uses these cases. In the mini-game below you find
the cause or the fix of each one.

{{< sim file="sims/disk-doctor.html" poster="sims/disk-doctor.png" title="Disk Doctor: file and device problems of a game" kind="game" height="520" >}}

Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, *Operating System Concepts*, 10th ed.,
Chapter 13 (file-system interface) and Chapter 12 (I/O systems). Microsoft
Support, "Update drivers manually in Windows".

## Exercises

1. What does a file system do? What is the metadata of a file?
2. Write the path of `slot1.sav` in Omar's Documents folder.
3. Why does a PC game keep the save file outside the game folder?
4. A file has 6 KB. Blocks are 4 KB. What is its size on disk?
5. 1 000 files of 1 KB each, blocks of 4 KB. How much space do they take on
   disk? How much as one pack?
6. Why can a FAT32 stick not take a 5 GB file?
7. Which format would you use for a USB stick for Windows and Mac?
8. What is a device driver? What does a yellow sign in Device Manager mean?
9. A phone charges on the PC, but the PC shows no files. What do you change?
10. Name four system resources that the OS shares between apps.

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. It keeps files and folders on a drive with their names, paths, sizes and dates; metadata is data about a file (name, type, size, dates, permissions).
2. `C:\Users\Omar\Documents\PocketQuest\Saves\slot1.sav`.
3. So that it stays when the game is updated or reinstalled.
4. 8 KB (2 blocks).
5. 4 000 KB (about 3.9 MB); as one pack 1 000 KB (250 blocks).
6. FAT32 allows no file of 4 GB or more.
7. exFAT.
8. A small program that lets the OS control one kind of hardware; the driver is missing or does not work.
9. The USB mode on the phone: file transfer.
10. For example CPU time, memory, storage, battery, network, devices.
:::
